brands.name: Raw Garden
brands.short: From the farm to the extract.
brands.text: Raw Garden traces its start to Santa Barbara County in 2015. Its own farm and extraction story is central to the brand: the company describes a seed-to-oil approach rather than sourcing a finished oil and placing a label on it.
brands.tip: Start with the extraction type. Refined live resin, live sauce and solventless live rosin are different product descriptions. Match the exact package to its published specifications before comparing price.
brands.question: Is this a cartridge, an all-in-one, or an extract that needs separate equipment?

brands.name: Kiva Confections
brands.text: Kiva is a California cannabis confectionery company with a portfolio spanning chocolates, gummies, mints and bites. Its product families include Kiva, Camino, Lost Farm, Petra and Terra. The name on the front of a package may therefore be a product family within a larger company.
brands.tip: Compare the individual piece and the whole package separately. Chocolate squares, mints and gummies are different formats, and a familiar brand name does not establish the amount in your particular package.
brands.question: What are the labeled milligrams per piece, and how many pieces are in this package?

brands.name: Camino
brands.short: Know the gummy behind the name.
brands.text: Camino is part of the Kiva portfolio. Its range includes gummies, sour gummies and fruit chews. The brand uses flavor, cannabinoid combinations and experience-oriented product names to distinguish its lines. Those names describe positioning, not a guaranteed personal response.
brands.tip: Read the exact variant. Products with similar artwork can carry different THC quantities or additional cannabinoids. Market-specific versions also differ, so use the California package and current local menu.
brands.question: Does this version contain CBD, CBN, CBG or another cannabinoid in addition to THC?

brands.name: WYLD
brands.short: Fruit-forward, with a label worth reading.
brands.text: WYLD presents itself as a nature-inspired edible brand built around fruit flavors. Its product range extends across multiple markets. For a San Jose shopper, the relevant comparison is the exact regulated California product rather than a package pictured on another state’s website.
brands.tip: Use ingredient lists to check dietary preferences. Compare cannabinoid ratios and package quantities before deciding that two flavors are equivalent. Flavor alone does not describe the full formulation.
brands.question: Am I comparing the same cannabinoid ratio and package size?

brands.name: PAX
brands.short: The device is part of the decision.
brands.text: PAX offers dry-herb vaporizers alongside oil-pod devices and cannabis products. Those are distinct systems. A device that uses loose flower is not the same as a battery designed for a prefilled oil pod.
brands.tip: Confirm hardware compatibility before buying. Look at the full device and pod names, whether a battery is included, and whether the item is a consumable product or reusable hardware.
brands.question: Will this product work with the device I already own?

brands.name: Jeeter
brands.text: Jeeter’s range includes pre-rolls and all-in-one vape products. Its own brand story emphasizes events, design and cannabis culture. When comparing its offerings, product construction is more informative than the size or color of a package.
brands.tip: Distinguish infused pre-rolls from flower-only products. Compare the number of units, total weight and ingredients. An all-in-one vape also has different replacement and disposal considerations from a rechargeable battery with a separate cartridge.
brands.question: What is added to the flower, and is the listed weight for one unit or the entire pack?

brands.name: Connected
brands.text: Connected traces its roots to Sacramento’s Fruitridge Health & Wellness Dispensary and describes launching the Connected brand in 2018. Its published history centers on cultivation and proprietary genetics, with a longstanding relationship with Alien Labs.
brands.tip: For flower, compare package date, batch information and weight alongside the cultivar name. A brand’s cultivation story gives context, but it cannot tell you the measured composition of every jar.
brands.question: Can I see the package date and the lab information for this exact batch?

brands.name: Alien Labs
brands.short: Genetics, culture, and the actual batch.
brands.text: Connected’s official history identifies Alien Labs as a longtime partner and a cultivation and lifestyle brand. The relationship is useful context for shoppers who see both names in a San Jose menu, but the brands should still be compared at the individual product level.
brands.tip: Do not treat cultivar names as fixed lab results. Check the product type, weight and batch documentation. Two packages with the same cultivar name can come from different harvests.
brands.question: Which characteristics are measured on the current batch, and which are general brand descriptions?

terpenes.name: Limonene
terpenes.text: Limonene is a useful starting point if you enjoy bright, peel-like aromas. This profile refers to the compound record identified below; limonene also has stereoisomers, which matter when interpreting chemical references.
terpenes.tip: A lemon-sounding cultivar name is not a limonene measurement. Ask for the terpene panel for the actual batch.

terpenes.name: Myrcene
terpenes.text: Myrcene is frequently discussed when people describe earthy, herbal cannabis aromas. Its presence is a chemical observation, not a reliable instruction about how a product will feel.
terpenes.tip: Compare its reported concentration with the rest of the panel. The largest individual terpene is only one part of a mixture.

terpenes.name: Alpha-pinene
terpenes.text: Alpha-pinene belongs to the pine-like end of the aroma vocabulary. Alpha-pinene and beta-pinene are distinct compounds, so a lab report may list them separately.
terpenes.tip: Keep alpha-pinene and beta-pinene separate when copying lab results. A combined pinene figure should say clearly that it combines both.

terpenes.name: Linalool
terpenes.text: Linalool is associated with floral fragrance descriptions. This guide uses floral as a sensory reference, not a claim that a cannabis product treats anxiety, sleep problems or any other condition.
terpenes.tip: Read the measured amount and the report units. A familiar floral association does not establish the dominant aroma of a whole product.

terpenes.name: Beta-caryophyllene
terpenes.text: Beta-caryophyllene sits in the spicy, woody part of this explorer. PubChem identifies it as a sesquiterpene, a different molecular class from monoterpenes such as myrcene.
terpenes.tip: Check whether the panel lists beta-caryophyllene or caryophyllene oxide. They are separate compounds and should not be merged without explanation.

terpenes.name: Humulene
terpenes.text: Humulene, also called alpha-caryophyllene, is a sesquiterpene. Its naming makes it easy to confuse with beta-caryophyllene, which has a different compound record.
terpenes.tip: Look for alternate names on reports. Avoid double-counting humulene and alpha-caryophyllene if a source uses both for the same compound.

terpenes.name: Terpinolene
terpenes.text: Terpinolene spans several aroma descriptors rather than fitting neatly into one box. The aroma chips in this explorer are editorial categories that help compare descriptions, not measured intensity scores.
terpenes.tip: A product can contain several terpenes with overlapping descriptors. Choose a profile to investigate, then check the current lab panel.

terpenes.name: Beta-pinene
terpenes.text: Beta-pinene is a distinct isomer of pinene. Sharing a molecular formula with another compound does not make the compounds identical or their sensory contributions interchangeable.
terpenes.tip: If a report says only pinene, ask whether it identifies an isomer or combines values. Record the laboratory’s wording exactly.

guides: terpene-panel-example
Read a terpene panel, one number at a time.
Worked example
An imaginary lab panel shows how units, missing values and totals fit together.
Begin with the report, not the cultivar name

Use a report that can be matched to the actual product and batch. Note the laboratory, sample or batch identifier and report date before copying individual values. A generic strain description cannot substitute for that match. This worked example uses invented numbers to explain arithmetic only; it is not a real product certificate or a quality benchmark.
Convert the units consistently

Suppose a panel reports limonene at 4 mg/g, myrcene at 2 mg/g and alpha-pinene at 1 mg/g. One percent equals 10 mg/g, so those values become 0.4%, 0.2% and 0.1%. The total of the three entered compounds is 0.7%, equivalent to 7 mg/g. Enter the three numbers in our converter with mg/g selected to reproduce this result. Do not combine some percentage values and some mg/g values in the same input mode.
Read the bar chart as a share of what you entered

Limonene accounts for about 57.1% of this entered three-compound total. That does not mean the product is 57.1% limonene. Its mass fraction in this example remains 0.4%. Our bars divide each entered value by the sum of entered values, while the numeric rows show the product-level concentrations. These two views answer different questions.
A blank is not a zero

If the report does not provide linalool, leave its field blank. A blank could reflect an unreported compound, a limited testing panel or information you have not copied yet. If a report uses ND, LOQ or another qualifier, consult its legend rather than translating the notation into a precise numeric zero. The converter intentionally counts entered fields and calls its sum the total of entered compounds.
Use the result to ask, not to predict

The arithmetic can help spot inconsistent units or compare panel structure. It cannot predict a person’s experience or establish overall product quality. Keep the original report alongside your calculations and ask the laboratory or retailer about unclear qualifiers. The compound records on our Sources page identify the molecules; they do not certify a specific package.
aroma-vocabulary
Build an aroma vocabulary that feels like yours.
Sensory field notes
Use everyday scent references to make a more precise description without inventing an effects score.
Start with a familiar reference

“Citrus” is a useful beginning, but citrus peel, juice and a sweet citrus candy are different mental references. Likewise, pine needles and dry wood share a broad neighborhood without being identical. Use ordinary food, herb and landscape memories to describe what a scent reminds you of. You do not need a laboratory vocabulary to record an observation clearly.
Choose a few descriptors rather than every descriptor

NOSE NOTES lets you select up to three aroma families. The limit makes the resulting card concise and easy to discuss. A citrus, floral and fresh combination might point you toward several overlapping compound profiles. The match uses any selected family, not a requirement that a single compound satisfy all three. The card is a record of your stated preferences, not a test of your sense of smell.
Separate liking from identification

You can like a pine-like smell without being able to identify alpha-pinene from smell alone. Real products are mixtures. Our categories provide a way to navigate published descriptions, while a batch-specific laboratory panel answers a chemical measurement question. Neither a flavor name nor a scent signature supplies a measured terpene concentration.
Make the conversation more specific

Try sharing your card with the prompt: “Which of these descriptions sounds most like you?” The recipient can open the same selection and change it to make their own. When comparing cards, talk about references rather than rankings. “I think of fresh orange peel” is more useful than saying one card is more advanced. No account, leaderboard or personal identity is required.
Bring the vocabulary back to the label

Once you have a few preferred words, explore the relevant compound pages and learn which names may appear on a panel. Keep alpha-pinene and beta-pinene distinct. Treat a descriptor match as a reason to investigate, and use the actual product documentation to find out what was measured. The editorial categories and chemical identifiers are explained on the Sources page.
terpene-myths
Five shortcuts that a terpene chart cannot justify.
Better interpretations
Learn where useful chemical information ends and an unsupported promise begins.
“The largest terpene decides everything”

The largest reported terpene is a fact about a particular panel, provided the units and sample are clear. It does not summarize every substance in a product or predict an individual response. Other measured and unmeasured components remain part of the product. Use a dominant value as a description of that report, not as a universal instruction.
“The strain name tells me the chemistry”

A name can be a helpful way to find a product, but it is not a batch certificate. Packages with the same cultivar name can originate from different harvests. A fruit word in the name is not a limonene measurement. If chemical composition matters to your comparison, match the actual package to its available laboratory documentation.
“A bigger total is always better”

A larger reported total is a larger reported total. It does not establish freshness, personal preference, safety or overall quality by itself. A total also depends on the panel: a sum across eight compounds is not automatically comparable with a sum across forty. Check which compounds were tested, which were included in the total and how values below reporting thresholds were handled.
“Shared formulas mean the same compound”

Several compounds can share a molecular formula while differing in structure. Alpha-pinene and beta-pinene should retain separate labels and values. Humulene may appear under its alternate name alpha-caryophyllene, which creates a different problem: counting the same compound twice. Record exact names and use the linked PubChem identifiers to resolve the reference.
“An aroma card is a wellness recommendation”

Our cards describe chosen vocabulary. They do not recommend treatment, dosing or a product for sleep, anxiety or pain. The shareable result deliberately stays with aromas and learning links. That makes it a useful conversation starter while keeping its claims aligned with the information entered. For health questions, seek appropriate professional guidance rather than treating a fragrance category as medical evidence.
glossary: mg/g
Milligrams per gram. Divide by ten to express the same mass fraction as percent.
Percent
Parts per hundred. One percent equals 10 mg/g.
Aroma family
An editorial scent category used here to navigate compound profiles.
Isomer
A compound sharing a molecular formula with another but having a different arrangement.
Terpene panel
The set of terpene measurements included in a particular report.
Entered total
The sum of only the numeric values you put into our converter.
ND
Often used for not detected. Consult the report’s own definition and reporting limits.
LOQ
Limit of quantification. Consult the laboratory’s methods and report legend.
PubChem CID
A compound identifier in the public PubChem database.
Scent signature
Your selected aroma preferences. It does not predict effects or prescribe a product.
